narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the admission model predicted a 58% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—a probability high enough to be considered a serious risk. In plain terms, the model looks at factors that historically separate students who pass from those who don't, and your profile raised more red flags than strengths.

The single most important factor in this decision was your academic standing in your third year of law school. You finished in the lowest decile of your class, placing you near the very bottom. By contrast, students who were accepted typically sat around the sixth decile. Because your third-year performance is a strong signal of legal knowledge and test readiness, this weighed heavily against you, pushing the prediction toward bar exam failure.

Your second most significant factor actually worked in your favor. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.90 is below the average of 3.23 among accepted students, but the model still treated it as a sign that you possess the intellectual foundation needed to succeed. This positive influence, however, was not enough to overcome your class rank.

The third factor was your enrollment status. You planned to attend law school part-time, whereas over 90% of accepted applicants studied full-time. The model associated part-time study with a higher risk of failing the bar, likely because balancing work and rigorous coursework can reduce exam preparation time. This pushed the prediction further toward failure.

To improve your chances on a future application, focus on raising your academic standing dramatically in your final year, consider switching to full-time study, and take bar preparation seriously. Your undergraduate GPA suggests capability—now show it through stronger law school performance and a dedicated, full-time commitment.
